etymology: Hebrew from Egyptian Pi-Tum, “house of Atum,” the sun-god of the setting sun; one of the two treasure-cities Israel built in bondage.
biblical_def: Pithom stands as the first monument of Israel's bondage, one of the two treasure-cities the enslaved Hebrews were compelled to build: “And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses” (Exo 1:11). Taskmasters were set over them to afflict them with their burdens, and the mortar and the brick of Pithom were tempered with the sweat and the groaning of the covenant people. Here Egypt shows her true face as the house of bondage, the iron furnace out of which the LORD would redeem His own. Yet the store-cities that Pharaoh reared for his own glory became the very stage of his overthrow, for the God of the Hebrews heard the cry that went up from those burdens; He heard their groaning, and remembered his covenant with Abraham. Pithom teaches the saint that affliction is not abandonment. The LORD suffered His people to labour in a strange land, but He numbered every burden and forgot not His covenant. So the church in every age builds, as it were, in the brickyards of the world, sighing under her burdens; yet her groaning is not lost, but ascends before the throne. The house of Atum, named for a dying sun, could not hold the people of the living God, whom He brought out with a stretched-out arm.
webster_summary: One of the two treasure-cities (Exo 1:11) that Israel built in bondage under the taskmasters; a monument of affliction, and of the covenant God who heard His people's groaning.
webster_full: PITHOM, a treasure-city of Egypt built by the enslaved Israelites (Exo 1:11).
Named for Atum, the setting sun-god; a store-city for Pharaoh's goods.
Reared under taskmasters set to afflict Israel with their burdens.
A monument of the house of bondage, the iron furnace of affliction.
Yet the LORD heard the groaning that rose from its brickyards, and remembered his covenant.
scriptures: Exo 1:11
Therefore they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens. And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses.
Exo 8:22
And I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.
Isa 43:3
For I am the LORD thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour: I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee.
Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God.
corruption_summary: A treasure-city of Israel's bondage; it recovers the truth that affliction is not abandonment, and that the covenant God hears the groaning of His people.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Pithom rebukes is the ancient lie of the taskmaster: that the people of God exist to serve the glory of the world's Pharaohs. Egypt built her treasure-cities on the backs of the enslaved, and every tyranny since has reckoned men as bricks for its own monuments. But the LORD reckons otherwise; He heard the groaning that rose from Pithom, and He remembered his covenant.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that affliction is not abandonment. The saint labouring under his burdens must not conclude that God has forgotten him. The LORD numbered every burden of His people in the brickyards of Egypt, and in His set time brought them out with a stretched-out arm. So He will bring out all His own from the house of bondage, for the covenant cannot fail.
roots_summary: The name joins the Egyptian pi (“house”) to the sun-god Atum; “house of Atum.”
roots_lines: Pithom — Egyptian Pi-Tum, “house of Atum.”
pi, the Egyptian word for “house” or “abode.”
Tum (Atum), the sun-god of the setting sun at Heliopolis.
Paired with Raamses as Pharaoh's two treasure-cities (Exo 1:11).
A store-city, from the sense of that which is laid up or treasured.
usage: Israel built Pithom and Raamses as treasure-cities for Pharaoh.
The taskmasters afflicted the Hebrews with burdens at Pithom.
The house of Atum could not hold the people of the living God.

etymology: Hebrew Baal-tsephon, “baal of the north”; a heathen idol reckoned lord of the winds and the sea, whose name the coastal place over against which Israel encamped bore.
biblical_def: Baal-zephon marks the last camp of Israel before the sea divided. The LORD Himself appointed the spot: “Speak unto the children of Israel, that they turn and encamp before Pihahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, over against Baalzephon” (Exo 14:2). The place was named for an idol, the baal of the north, whom the heathen worshipped as lord of the winds and the waters. Hither Pharaoh pursued, thinking the wilderness had shut Israel in and that his gods had delivered them into his hand: “But the Egyptians pursued after them…and overtook them encamping by the sea, beside Pihahiroth, before Baalzephon” (Exo 14:9). Yet it was at the very shrine of the sea-god that the LORD got Himself the victory. He drove back the sea by a strong east wind, He made the depths a highway for His redeemed, and He overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the midst of the waters. The idol lord of the sea stood by, dumb and impotent, while the God of Israel ruled the deep. So the LORD executed judgment against all the gods of Egypt (Exo 12:12), and did it at the place that bore an idol's name, that none might doubt whose arm had wrought the salvation. Baal-zephon preaches that the LORD triumphs over the false gods on their own ground, and saves His people through the very sea that swallows their enemies.
webster_summary: The shore-place, named for a heathen sea-idol, over against which Israel encamped before the crossing (Exo 14:2); where the LORD triumphed over Egypt's gods at the very sea.
webster_full: BAAL-ZEPHON, a place on the Red Sea shore over against which Israel encamped (Exo 14:2).
Named for an idol, the “baal of the north,” reckoned lord of the sea and winds.
There Pharaoh overtook Israel encamping by the sea (Exo 14:9).
At that idol's shrine the LORD divided the deep and drowned the host of Egypt.
A witness that the LORD triumphs over the false gods on their own ground.
scriptures: Exo 14:2
Speak unto the children of Israel, that they turn and encamp before Pihahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, over against Baalzephon: before it shall ye encamp by the sea.
Exo 14:9
But the Egyptians pursued after them, all the horses and chariots of Pharaoh, and his horsemen, and his army, and overtook them encamping by the sea, beside Pihahiroth, before Baalzephon.
Isa 19:1

The burden of Egypt. Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt: and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst of it.
Psa 96:5
For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens.
corruption_summary: A place named for a heathen sea-idol where the LORD triumphed over Egypt's gods; it rebukes the vanity of every idol that pretends to rule what God alone commands.
corruption_paragraphs: Baal-zephon was a shrine of open idolatry. The heathen bowed to a baal of the north as lord of the winds and the waters, ascribing to a dumb image the dominion that belongs to the living God alone. This is the root of all idolatry: to take the glory of the Creator, who made the sea and the dry land, and lay it upon the works of men's hands. “For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens” (Psa 96:5).

The LORD answered that idolatry not with argument but with the sea. At the very place that bore the idol's name He divided the waters, saved His people, and drowned Pharaoh's host; the baal of the sea could not still one wave. Let the church learn to fear no idol, however dread its name or ancient its worship. The idols of Egypt were moved at His presence (Isa 19:1), and the God who ruled the deep at Baal-zephon rules it still. Worship Him alone who made the heavens.
roots_summary: The name compounds baal (“lord, master”) with tsephon (“north”); the idol-lord of the north.
roots_lines: Baal-zephon — Hebrew Baal-tsephon, “baal of the north.”
baal, “lord, master, husband,” the common Canaanite idol-name.
tsephon, “north,” from a root meaning to hide or lay up.
The idol was reckoned lord of the sea-winds and storms.
The place on Egypt's eastern shore took the idol's name (Exo 14:2).
usage: Israel encamped before Baal-zephon by the sea.
Pharaoh overtook them beside Pihahiroth, before Baal-zephon.
At Baal-zephon the LORD overthrew the gods of Egypt.

etymology: Hebrew On, from Egyptian Iunu, “city of the pillar”; the ancient centre of sun-worship the Greeks called Heliopolis, the city of the sun.
biblical_def: On was the city of the sun, the great seat of Egypt's sun-worship, called by the Greeks Heliopolis. It was into a house of this city that Joseph was married when Pharaoh exalted him: “And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphnathpaaneah; and he gave him to wife Asenath the daughter of Potipherah priest of On” (Gen 41:45). Of that marriage were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath “the daughter of Potipherah priest of On bare unto him” (Gen 46:20). Here is the deep providence of God, that in the very city of the sun-idol, in the household of its priest, the LORD planted the sons who would become two tribes of Israel. Joseph walked as a light in the heart of pagan Egypt, keeping his integrity in Potiphar's house and his faith in Pharaoh's court, so that the God of his fathers was glorified where the sun was adored. The city of the sun could not eclipse the true Light; rather the LORD made Joseph a saviour of nations in the midst of it. On teaches that God's elect are often set down in dark places, married as it were to the world's circumstances, yet kept and used for the building of the covenant people. The sun of Heliopolis has long set; the seed of Joseph endures, and the Sun of Righteousness has arisen with healing in His wings.
webster_summary: The city of the sun (Heliopolis), whose priest Potipherah gave Joseph his wife Asenath (Gen 41:45); a witness to God's providence keeping His own in the heart of pagan Egypt.
webster_full: ON, the Egyptian city of the sun, called by the Greeks Heliopolis (Gen 41:45).
Its priest Potipherah gave his daughter Asenath to Joseph.
There Manasseh and Ephraim, two tribes of Israel, were born (Gen 46:20).
A centre of sun-worship, yet a place of God's hidden providence.
The city of the sun could not eclipse the true Light.
scriptures: And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphnathpaaneah; and he gave him to wife Asenath the daughter of Potipherah priest of On. And Joseph went out over all the land of Egypt.
And unto Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, which Asenath the daughter of Potipherah priest of On bare unto him.
Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God.
Whom the LORD of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance.
corruption_summary: The city of the sun-idol where God's providence kept Joseph and planted two tribes of Israel; it rebukes the worship of the creature and exalts the true Light.
corruption_paragraphs: On was the very throne of sun-worship, where the creature was adored in the place of the Creator. Men bowed to the burning disc and served the host of heaven, exchanging the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of a made thing. Scripture names this the root sin of the heathen, to worship and serve the creature more than the Creator; and Egypt's sun-city was its ancient citadel.

Yet even into that citadel the LORD sent His light, keeping Joseph faithful in the priest's own household and raising up out of it two tribes of Israel. The prophet foresaw the day when Egypt should turn: “Blessed be Egypt my people” (Isa 19:25), and princes should come out of Egypt to stretch their hands unto God (Psa 68:31). The sun of On has set; the Sun of Righteousness shines. Turn from the dying idol to the living Light, and worship the Creator, who is blessed for ever.
roots_summary: On renders Egyptian Iunu, “city of the pillar”; the Greeks named it Heliopolis, “city of the sun.”
roots_lines: On — Hebrew from Egyptian Iunu, “place of pillars.”
Greek Heliopolis, “city of the sun.”
The chief seat of Egyptian sun-worship, the god Ra.
Its priest was Potipherah, father of Asenath (Gen 41:45).
Called Aven in Eze 30:17, a scornful pointing at its vanity.
usage: Joseph married Asenath, daughter of the priest of On.
On was the Egyptian city of the sun, later Heliopolis.
In the city of the sun-idol God kept His servant Joseph.

etymology: Hebrew Tsoan, perhaps “place of departure” or “removal”; the ancient royal city of the Nile delta the Greeks called Tanis.
biblical_def: Zoan was among the most ancient of Egypt's royal cities, so old that Scripture dates the founding of Hebron by it: Hebron “was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt” (Num 13:22). It was the theatre of the LORD's mighty acts against Pharaoh, the field where the plagues were wrought: “Marvellous things did he in the sight of their fathers, in the land of Egypt, in the field of Zoan” (Psa 78:12), and again, “how he had wrought his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the field of Zoan” (Psa 78:43). Here the God of the Hebrews turned the rivers to blood, sent the darkness and the death of the firstborn, and made a mockery of Egypt's wisdom before her king. For all her ancient glory and her boasted counsellors, Zoan is exposed as the seat of folly: “Surely the princes of Zoan are fools, the counsel of the wise counsellors of Pharaoh is become brutish” (Isa 19:11). The princes vaunted themselves the sons of the wise and of ancient kings, yet before the wisdom of God they were fools. Zoan teaches that the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. The oldest and craftiest counsel of men cannot stand against the LORD; He wrought His wonders in their own field, and made the sages of the Nile confess a hand mightier than all their arts.
webster_summary: The ancient royal city (Tanis), the field of the LORD's wonders against Egypt (Psa 78:12), whose princes are exposed as fools (Isa 19:11); a witness that worldly wisdom is folly with God.
webster_full: ZOAN, an ancient royal city of the Nile delta, the Greek Tanis (Num 13:22).
Built seven years after Hebron, a mark of its antiquity.
The field where the LORD wrought His wonders against Egypt (Psa 78:12, 43).
Its wise counsellors are pronounced fools and brutish (Isa 19:11).
A monument that the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God.
scriptures: And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)
Marvellous things did he in the sight of their fathers, in the land of Egypt, in the field of Zoan.
How he had wrought his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the field of Zoan:
Surely the princes of Zoan are fools, the counsel of the wise counsellors of Pharaoh is become brutish: how say ye unto Pharaoh, I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings?
corruption_summary: The ancient royal city whose wise counsellors were made fools; it recovers the truth that the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Zoan displays is the pride of human wisdom that will not bow to God. Her princes boasted themselves the sons of the wise and of ancient kings, yet their vaunted counsel was become brutish before the LORD. So it is in every age: the learned of the world set their reason above revelation and are made fools in the very field of their boasting.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. The LORD wrought His wonders in the field of Zoan, and the sages of Egypt could neither foretell nor withstand them. Let no man trust the counsel of the crafty against the plain word of God. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand, when the wise counsellors of Pharaoh are proved fools.
roots_summary: Tsoan is thought to bear the sense of loading up and journeying, hence “place of departure”; the Greeks called it Tanis.
roots_lines: Zoan — Hebrew Tsoan, perhaps “place of removal” or “departure.”
Identified with Tanis, a royal city of the eastern delta.
Its antiquity fixed by comparison with Hebron (Num 13:22).
Called “the field of Zoan” as the arena of the plagues (Psa 78:12).
A byword for Egypt's proud but foolish counsel (Isa 19:11).
usage: Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.
The LORD wrought His wonders in the field of Zoan.
The princes of Zoan are fools before the wisdom of God.

etymology: Hebrew Noph, a contraction of Egyptian Men-nefer; Memphis, the ancient capital of lower Egypt and chief seat of her idols.
biblical_def: Noph, the Memphis of the Greeks, was the ancient capital of lower Egypt and the great storehouse of her idols. Isaiah joins her to Zoan in the indictment of Egypt's leaders: “The princes of Zoan are become fools, the princes of Noph are deceived; they have also seduced Egypt, even they that are the stay of the tribes thereof” (Isa 19:13). The men who should have upheld the nation deceived it, being themselves deceived, for they leaned upon their gods and their own craft rather than the living God. Jeremiah names her among the cities that fed upon Judah in her calamity: “Also the children of Noph and Tahapanes have broken the crown of thy head” (Jer 2:16). But the surest word over Noph is the sentence of the LORD upon her idols: “I will also destroy the idols, and I will cause their images to cease out of Noph; and there shall be no more a prince of the land of Egypt: and I will put a fear in the land of Egypt” (Eze 30:13). The city that housed the images could not preserve them; the God of Israel cut them off and left her princeless. Noph preaches the certain doom of idolatry. However venerable the temple, however cunning the counsel that guards it, the LORD will make the images to cease and put His fear in the land, that men may know there is no god beside Him.
webster_summary: Memphis, the ancient capital and chief seat of Egypt's idols, whose images the LORD swore to destroy (Eze 30:13); a witness to the certain doom of idolatry.
webster_full: NOPH, the ancient capital of lower Egypt, the Memphis of the Greeks (Isa 19:13).
The great seat of Egypt's idols and their images.
Its deceived princes seduced the nation (Isa 19:13).
The LORD swore to destroy the idols and cause the images to cease (Eze 30:13).
A witness to the certain doom of idolatry.
scriptures: The princes of Zoan are become fools, the princes of Noph are deceived; they have also seduced Egypt, even they that are the stay of the tribes thereof.
Jer 2:16
Also the children of Noph and Tahapanes have broken the crown of thy head.

Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also destroy the idols, and I will cause their images to cease out of Noph; and there shall be no more a prince of the land of Egypt: and I will put a fear in the land of Egypt.
And I will set fire in Egypt: Sin shall have great pain, and No shall be rent asunder, and Noph shall have distresses daily.
corruption_summary: The chief seat of Egypt's idols, doomed by the LORD; it rebukes idolatry and the deceived leaders who trust in images rather than the living God.
corruption_paragraphs: Noph was the great house of Egypt's images, where the idols were served and the people taught to trust in them. Her princes were not merely mistaken but deceived, and deceiving; leaning on gods that could not save, they seduced the tribes that looked to them for a stay. Idolatry is never harmless error, for it blinds the leaders and betrays the led.

Against this the LORD pronounced a sentence that no temple could avert: “I will also destroy the idols, and I will cause their images to cease out of Noph” (Eze 30:13). The images that were the city's pride became her shame; He cut them off and put His fear in the land. So shall it be with every idol and every idol-priest that stands against the living God. Let men cast away their images and fear the LORD alone, before He make their glory to cease and rend their city asunder.
roots_summary: Noph shortens the Egyptian Men-nefer, “enduring and beautiful”; also written Moph, the Greek Memphis.
roots_lines: Noph — Hebrew for Egyptian Men-nefer, “enduring, beautiful.”
Also written Moph (Hos 9:6); the Greek Memphis.
The ancient capital of lower Egypt, near modern Cairo.
A chief centre of idol-worship, the temple of Ptah.
Doomed with her images by the word of the LORD (Eze 30:13).
usage: The princes of Noph are deceived, saith the prophet.
The LORD would cause the images to cease out of Noph.
Noph shall have distresses daily in the day of judgment.

etymology: Hebrew Tachpanches (also Tehaphnehes, Tahapanes); a fortified frontier city of the eastern Nile delta, the Greek Daphnae.
biblical_def: Tahpanhes was a fortress city on Egypt's eastern frontier, the first great stronghold that met a traveller coming up out of Judah. Thither the remnant of Judah fled after the fall of Jerusalem, dragging the prophet Jeremiah with them against the plain word of the LORD: “So they came into the land of Egypt: for they obeyed not the voice of the LORD: thus came they even to Tahpanhes” (Jer 43:7). They thought to find safety under Pharaoh's shield, but they fled from the sword only to meet it, for the word of the LORD pursued them: “Declare ye in Egypt, and publish in Migdol, and publish in Noph and in Tahpanhes: say ye, Stand fast, and prepare thee; for the sword shall devour round about thee” (Jer 46:14). At Tahpanhes the LORD would set the conqueror's throne, and there He would break the yokes of Egypt: “At Tehaphnehes also the day shall be darkened, when I shall break there the yokes of Egypt” (Eze 30:18). Tahpanhes preaches the folly of fleeing to Egypt against the counsel of God. There is no refuge from the hand of the LORD in the house of Pharaoh, no wall thick enough to keep out His sword. They that forsake His word to trust in the arm of flesh do but carry their judgment with them; the fortress of Egypt becomes the seat of the conqueror's throne.
webster_summary: A fortified frontier city of the Nile delta where the fleeing Judeans took Jeremiah against the LORD's word (Jer 43:7); a witness to the folly of trusting Egypt against God.
webster_full: TAHPANHES, a fortress city of Egypt's eastern frontier (Jer 43:7).
Also called Tehaphnehes and Tahapanes; the Greek Daphnae.
Thither the remnant of Judah fled, taking Jeremiah with them.
There the LORD would set the conqueror's throne and break Egypt's yokes (Eze 30:18).
A witness to the folly of fleeing to Egypt against the word of God.

At Tehaphnehes also the day shall be darkened , when I shall break there the yokes of Egypt: and the pomp of her strength shall cease in her: as for her, a cloud shall cover her, and her daughters shall go into captivity.
Jer 44:1
The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews which dwell in the land of Egypt, which dwell at Migdol, and at Tahpanhes, and at Noph, and in the country of Pathros, saying,
corruption_summary: The frontier fortress where Judah fled for refuge against God's word; it recovers the folly of trusting the arm of flesh and forsaking the counsel of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Tahpanhes rebukes is the ancient sin of seeking refuge anywhere but in God. The remnant of Judah feared the sword of Babylon and fled to Egypt's fortress, forsaking the express command of the LORD, who had promised to keep them if they stayed. To trust the arm of flesh against the plain word of God is unbelief clothed as prudence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that there is no refuge from the hand of the LORD but the LORD Himself. Pharaoh's walls could not keep out His sword; He set the throne of the conqueror in the fortress of the fugitives. Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help and stay on horses. The saint must not flee God's discipline into the world's strongholds, but cast himself upon the mercy and the promise of Him whose word cannot fail.
roots_summary: Tachpanches is an Egyptian frontier name; the Greeks called the garrison Daphnae.
roots_lines: Tahpanhes — Hebrew Tachpanches, an Egyptian frontier name.
Also Tehaphnehes (Eze 30:18) and Tahapanes (Jer 2:16).
The Greek Daphnae, a garrison on the eastern delta.
A refuge sought by the fleeing remnant of Judah (Jer 43:7).
The seat of the conqueror's throne by the LORD's word.
usage: The remnant of Judah came even to Tahpanhes.
Publish in Noph and in Tahpanhes, saith the LORD.
At Tahpanhes the day shall be darkened when God breaks Egypt's yokes.

etymology: Hebrew Pi-beseth, from Egyptian Per-Bast, “house of Bast”; the delta city of the cat-goddess, the Greek Bubastis.
biblical_def: Pibeseth, the Bubastis of the Greeks, was a delta city given over to the worship of the goddess Bast, her house and shrine. Ezekiel names her in the roll of Egypt's cities appointed to the sword in the day of the LORD's visitation: “The young men of Aven and of Pibeseth shall fall by the sword: and these cities shall go into captivity” (Eze 30:17). The strength of a city is her young men, and it is her young men the LORD marks for the sword; the pride of the Nile should fall in the flower of her age, and the city of the cat-goddess should go into captivity. So the prophet sets Pibeseth beside Aven, which is On the sun-city, that the two great seats of Egypt's idol-worship might fall together, the house of the sun and the house of Bast alike. Pibeseth preaches the day of the LORD upon the cities of Egypt. He has a controversy with the idol-cities, and His sword is whetted against their pride. No temple of the beast-gods, no multitude of young and strong defenders, can turn back the sentence of the God who lives. When His day dawns upon a proud and idolatrous city, her young men fall and her people go into captivity, that men may know the LORD is God, and the idols are nothing.
webster_summary: Bubastis, the delta city of the cat-goddess Bast, whose young men should fall by the sword (Eze 30:17); a witness to the day of the LORD upon the idol-cities of Egypt.
webster_full: PIBESETH, an Egyptian delta city, the Bubastis of the Greeks (Eze 30:17).
From Per-Bast, “house of Bast,” the cat-goddess.
A seat of idol-worship, set beside Aven (On) by the prophet.
Her young men appointed to fall by the sword, her people to captivity.
A witness to the day of the LORD upon the cities of Egypt.

Zep 2:11
The LORD will be terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and men shall worship him, every one from his place, even all the isles of the heathen.
corruption_summary: The city of the cat-goddess Bast, appointed to the sword; it rebukes the idolatry of the beast-gods and proclaims the day of the LORD upon the proud idol-cities.
corruption_paragraphs: Pibeseth was the house of a beast-god, where men bowed to the image of a cat and kept festival to a creature they had made a deity. Egypt filled her pantheon with the shapes of beasts and birds, and Pibeseth was among the chief of these shrines. This is idolatry sunk to its depths, when the glory of God is changed into an image made like to fourfooted beasts and creeping things.

The LORD's answer is the sword and the day of visitation: her young men shall fall, and the city shall go into captivity. He has purposed to famish all the gods of the earth: “The LORD will be terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and men shall worship him, every one from his place” (Zep 2:11). The beast-gods of Egypt could not save one youth of Pibeseth. Let men forsake the idols, however festive their worship, and bow to the living God, before whom every false god shall wither in the day of His terror.
roots_summary: Pibeseth renders Egyptian Per-Bast, “house of Bast”; the Greeks called it Bubastis.
roots_lines: Pibeseth — Egyptian Per-Bast, “house of Bast.”
Bast (Bastet), the cat-goddess of the delta.
The Greek Bubastis, a great festival city on the Nile.
Set beside Aven (On) among the doomed idol-cities (Eze 30:17).
Her young men marked for the sword in the day of the LORD.
usage: The young men of Pibeseth shall fall by the sword.
Pibeseth was the house of the cat-goddess Bast.
The day of the LORD came upon the idol-cities of Egypt.

etymology: Hebrew Pathros, from Egyptian Pa-to-res, “the land of the south”; Upper Egypt, reckoned the ancient cradle of the nation.
biblical_def: Pathros is Upper Egypt, the southern land the Egyptians held to be the origin of their nation. Thither the obstinate remnant of Judah pressed on, past the frontier fortresses into the heart of Egypt, and there the word of the LORD found them: “The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews which dwell in the land of Egypt…and in the country of Pathros” (Jer 44:1). In Pathros the fugitives hardened themselves in idolatry, burning incense to the queen of heaven and refusing the prophet's rebuke, so that the LORD set His face against them for evil. Ezekiel numbers Pathros among the cities appointed to desolation: “And I will make Pathros desolate, and will set fire in Zoan, and will execute judgments in No” (Eze 30:14). Yet Pathros is not left without hope, for it stands also in the great promise of the second gathering: “the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people…from Egypt, and from Pathros” (Isa 11:11). Here is the wonder of grace, that the very land where the remnant sinned so grievously is named among the places from which the LORD will yet gather His own. Pathros preaches both the peril of hardened idolatry and the reach of sovereign mercy. Judgment fell upon the obstinate; yet the outstretched hand that scattered will gather again, and no corner of the earth is beyond the LORD's recovering grace.
webster_summary: Upper Egypt, whither the Judean remnant fled to burn incense to the queen of heaven (Jer 44:1); appointed to desolation, yet named among the lands from which the LORD will gather His own (Isa 11:11).
webster_full: PATHROS, Upper Egypt, the southern land (Jer 44:1).
Reckoned by the Egyptians the ancient cradle of their nation.
Whither the Judean remnant fled and hardened in idolatry.
Appointed to desolation with Zoan and No (Eze 30:14).
Yet named among the lands of the second gathering (Isa 11:11).
scriptures: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.
Jer 44:1
The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews which dwell in the land of Egypt, which dwell at Migdol, and at Tahpanhes, and at Noph, and in the country of Pathros, saying,
And I will make Pathros desolate, and will set fire in Zoan, and will execute judgments in No.
Whom the LORD of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance.
corruption_summary: Upper Egypt, where the fleeing remnant burned incense to the queen of heaven; it rebukes obstinate idolatry, yet proclaims the reach of the LORD's recovering mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: In Pathros the remnant of Judah fell into open and defiant idolatry, burning incense and pouring drink offerings to the queen of heaven, and when Jeremiah rebuked them they answered that they would not hearken but would perform their vows. This is idolatry grown insolent, when men take God's own preservation as licence to serve false gods, and prefer the abominable rites of the heathen to the plain word of the LORD.

For such hardness the LORD made Pathros desolate; the queen of heaven could deliver none of her worshippers. Yet even here mercy is not shut up, for the same hand that scattered will gather “the second time…from Egypt, and from Pathros” (Isa 11:11), and the day is promised when the LORD shall say, “Blessed be Egypt my people” (Isa 19:25). Forsake the queen of heaven and turn to the King of heaven, whose recovering grace reaches even to the land of obstinate idols.
roots_summary: Pathros renders Egyptian Pa-to-res, “the land of the south”; Upper Egypt, whence the Pathrusim of Gen 10:14.
roots_lines: Pathros — Egyptian Pa-to-res, “land of the south.”
Upper Egypt, from the first cataract northward toward Memphis.
The Pathrusim descend from it (Gen 10:14).
A refuge of the fleeing remnant of Judah (Jer 44:1).
Both doomed (Eze 30:14) and named in the second gathering (Isa 11:11).
usage: The Jews that dwelt in the country of Pathros burned incense to idols.
The LORD would make Pathros desolate.
From Pathros the LORD will gather the remnant of His people.

etymology: Hebrew Sin, rendered Pelusium in the margin; a fortified city on Egypt's north-eastern coast, called “the strength of Egypt” (distinct from the wilderness of Sin).
biblical_def: Sin, which the margin renders Pelusium, was the great fortress on Egypt's north-eastern coast, the key that locked the land against invaders from the east. So the LORD names her “the strength of Egypt,” and against that strength He pledged His fury: “And I will pour my fury upon Sin, the strength of Egypt; and I will cut off the multitude of No” (Eze 30:15). The mightiest bulwark of the land was singled out for the fiercest stroke, that when the strong place fell all Egypt might see her helplessness. The prophet presses it home: “Sin shall have great pain, and No shall be rent asunder, and Noph shall have distresses daily” (Eze 30:16). This city must not be confounded with the wilderness of Sin through which Israel journeyed toward Sinai; it is a different place bearing a like name, a walled fortress of the delta and not a desert of the wandering. Sin preaches that the strength of the nations is no strength against the LORD. Men fortify their frontiers and name their bastions their confidence, but the God of Israel pours out His fury and the fortress is filled with pain. When He determines to break a proud people, He strikes first at the thing they trust; the strength of Egypt is weakness before the Almighty, and no wall can stand where His fury is poured out.
webster_summary: Pelusium, the frontier fortress called “the strength of Egypt,” on which the LORD would pour His fury (Eze 30:15); a witness that the strength of nations is nothing before God (distinct from the wilderness of Sin).
webster_full: SIN (EGYPT), a frontier fortress of Egypt, the Pelusium of the margin (Eze 30:15).
Called “the strength of Egypt,” guarding the north-eastern coast.
On it the LORD swore to pour out His fury.
Distinct from the wilderness of Sin on the way to Sinai.
A witness that the strength of nations is nothing before God.
scriptures: And I will pour my fury upon Sin, the strength of Egypt; and I will cut off the multitude of No.
And I will set fire in Egypt: Sin shall have great pain, and No shall be rent asunder, and Noph shall have distresses daily.
Behold, therefore I am against thee, and against thy rivers, and I will make the land of Egypt utterly waste and desolate, from the tower of Syene even unto the border of Ethiopia.
Nah 3:9
Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite ; Put and Lubim were thy helpers.
corruption_summary: The fortress called the strength of Egypt, doomed to the LORD's fury; it recovers the truth that no bulwark of the nations can stand against the Almighty.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Sin rebukes is the trust of the nations in their own strength. Egypt reckoned this fortress her surety, the strong key that kept the enemy from her gates, and named it her confidence. Men do ever the same, making a god of their defences and a boast of their walls, as though flesh could bar the door against the judgment of heaven.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the strength of the nations is weakness before the LORD. He pledged to pour His fury upon the strength of Egypt, and the fortress was filled with pain. When God arises to judge, He strikes first at the thing men trust, that their confidence may be turned to terror. Let no people, and no soul, rest in the arm of flesh; the LORD alone is a strong tower, and the fortress that is not founded on Him shall be rent asunder.
roots_summary: Sin here is the fortress-city, marginally Pelusium, from a name suggesting mire or clay; not to be confounded with the desert of Sin.
roots_lines: Sin (Egypt) — a delta fortress, marginally Pelusium (Eze 30:15).
The name is thought to bear the sense of “mire” or “clay.”
Called “the strength of Egypt,” her eastern gate.
Distinct from the wilderness of Sin (Exo 16:1).
Appointed to the fury of the LORD in the day of Egypt's fall.
usage: The LORD would pour His fury upon Sin, the strength of Egypt.
Sin shall have great pain in the day of judgment.
This Sin is a fortress, not the wilderness of the wandering.

etymology: Hebrew No Amon, “the city of Amon”; Thebes, the great capital of Upper Egypt, seat of the god Amon, called by Nahum “populous No.”
biblical_def: No, or No Amon, was Thebes, the mighty capital of Upper Egypt and the chief seat of the god Amon, from whom she took her name. Nahum holds her up as a warning to Nineveh, that no greatness can secure a city against the judgment of God: “Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?” (Nah 3:8). She was defended by her waters and buttressed by mighty allies—“Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers” (Nah 3:9)—yet for all her rivers and her ramparts she fell, and her people went into captivity. The LORD had marked her for judgment with her false god: “Behold, I will punish the multitude of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with their gods, and their kings” (Jer 46:25), and Ezekiel joined her to the desolation: “I will…execute judgments in No” (Eze 30:14). No preaches the certainty of judgment upon the proud, be they never so great. She trusted her waters, her walls, and her infinite allies, and her god Amon could not save her. If populous No, with the sea for her rampart, was rent asunder, no Nineveh, no Babylon, no city of man can stand against the LORD. The God who punished No and her gods will surely visit every proud and idolatrous people that exalts itself against Him.
webster_summary: Thebes, “populous No,” the great city of the god Amon, whose fall Nahum sets as a warning to Nineveh (Nah 3:8); a witness to the certainty of judgment on the proud.
webster_full: NO (AMON), Thebes, the great capital of Upper Egypt (Nah 3:8).
Named for the god Amon, her chief idol.
Defended by her rivers and by mighty allies, yet she fell.
The LORD punished No with her gods and her kings (Jer 46:25).
A warning that no greatness secures a city against God's judgment.
scriptures: Nah 3:8
Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?
The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, saith; Behold, I will punish the multitude of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with their gods, and their kings; even Pharaoh, and all them that trust in him:
And I will make Pathros desolate, and will set fire in Zoan, and will execute judgments in No.
Nah 3:9
Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite ; Put and Lubim were thy helpers.
corruption_summary: Thebes, the city of the god Amon, whose fall warns the proud; it rebukes the idolatry and self-trust of great cities, and proclaims the certainty of God's judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: No took her very name from her idol, the god Amon, and made him her boast and her defence. She trusted a false god and her own greatness together, her rivers, her ramparts, and her infinite allies, as though the sum of them could ward off heaven. This is the double corruption of the proud city: idolatry within her temples and self-sufficiency within her walls.

The LORD punished No with her gods and her kings, and populous Thebes was rent asunder and led captive; Amon could not save the city that bore his name. Nahum set her ruin before Nineveh, and it stands before every proud people still: “Art thou better than populous No?” No idol can shield, no rampart can hold, when the LORD arises to judge. Let the nations cast down their idols and humble their pride, and let the church trust not in numbers or in walls, but in the living God, who bringeth the great city low.
roots_summary: No is the Hebrew name for Thebes; Amon is her god, so “No of Amon,” the city of that idol.
roots_lines: No (Amon) — Hebrew No Amon, “the city of Amon.”
No, the Hebrew name for Thebes of Upper Egypt.
Amon, the chief god of Thebes, her namesake idol.
Called “populous No” for her multitude (Nah 3:8).
Her fall a byword of judgment on the proud (Jer 46:25).
usage: Art thou better than populous No, saith the prophet to Nineveh.
Ethiopia and Egypt were the strength of No, yet she fell.
The LORD punished the multitude of No with her gods.
